items.summary: The Nvidia board voted unanimously Monday to reinstate Jensen Huang as the company's president, CEO and fellow director, a reversal from just six days earlier when members had accepted his resignation after he admitted an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. The announcement stated the decision followed discussions with Huang and input from senior levels of the U.S. government; President Donald Trump said he believes his intervention was crucial to bringing Huang back. The board's reversal has drawn scrutiny over its independence and the meeting of business and politics, raising questions about corporate governance and Trump's role in the matter. Lawmakers have called for accountability: Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren, incoming chair of the Senate Banking Committee, called the reinstatement "reckless" while noting Huang, Nvidia executives and the board still owe Congress answers; Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand demanded that both Huang and the board testify publicly to Congress, stating a boardroom vote does not resolve a national security risk. California Attorney General Rob Bonta said Tuesday in an interview with CNBC that Trump's intervention "does not bode well for enforcement of the law by the federal government without fear, without favor." The California Department of Justice asked Nvidia Thursday whether its advanced chips or confidential information may have gone to China and whether it misled investors and the public. The board includes long-serving members such as Mark Stevens and Tench Coxe, who joined in 1993 when Nvidia was founded; chairman Harvey Jones and CFO Brooke Seawell from Synopsys (Jones since 1993, Seawell four years later); lead independent director Stephen Neal, who joined in 2019; and others with less direct ties to the company. None of the board members commented on requests from The Associated Press.
items.title: Nvidia Board That Reinstated Jensen Huang Now Under Scrutiny

items.summary: On Monday, Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive officer under pressure from President Trump, reversing his resignation over revelations of extramarital affairs involving Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive accused of ties to Chinese intelligence. The decision drew Wall Street support but alarmed some U.S. officials and lawmakers who warned it endangered national security. Senator Tom Cotton, the Republican chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, said on social media that "the controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg" because Huang had regained his job. Trump celebrated the return in a CNBC interview, calling Huang a "national treasure" and stating after research that there was no national security problem. The Commerce Department added Megaspeed and other firms to a trade blacklist on Monday. Princeton professor Aaron Friedberg said the intervention would trigger broader tightening of restrictions beyond Nvidia and China. Three bills advancing through Congress—the AI Overwatch Act, Chip Security Act, and Match Act—would further restrict Chinese access to semiconductors; DGA-Albright Stonebridge Group's Paul Triolo warned the Match Act could breach a red line set by Xi Jinping and provoke retaliation. Democrats are expected to control large majorities in both chambers after January 3, potentially overriding Trump vetoes even if restrictions do not pass before end of 2026. Center for American Progress senior fellow Michael Schiffer noted China has been slow to buy chips despite export controls. Asia Society Policy Institute expert Lizzi C. Lee said Beijing is unlikely to rely on U.S. goodwill and that domestic chip substitution efforts would accelerate after this episode exposed vulnerabilities in China's AI ambitions.
items.title: Nvidia Reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO Amid Ongoing US-China Chip Tensions

items.summary: According to a Wednesday report by Fortune, citing people familiar with the discussions, Amazon and Meta have held multiple rounds of talks about allowing Meta's popular AI agent, Muse, to connect directly to Amazon's store. The reported negotiations would mark a significant reversal from just two months ago, when Muse users were unable to purchase products on Amazon and instead received an error message when attempting to check out. Two key issues remain under negotiation: how search results would be presented and how advertising would be handled under a potential agreement. One of Amazon's biggest concerns is how third-party shopping agents like Muse could affect its advertising business; in October, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy argued that few customers were making purchases through outside shopping agents. Amazon may also have been waiting for Muse to mature before agreeing to integrate it with its marketplace, since if Muse places the wrong order or creates a problem with a purchase, Amazon could be left dealing with frustrated customers and unhappy sellers. Fortune reported that executives are concerned that third-party shopping agents could weaken Amazon's direct relationship with consumers. Any potential agreement between Amazon and Meta would reportedly require approval from both companies' CEOs. Meta and Amazon have not yet responded to TechCrunch's requests for comment.
items.title: Amazon and Meta Reportedly in Talks to Lift Blockade on AI Agent Muse

items.summary: The sharp stock rally following Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's return has quickly dissipated. Shares surged 31% on Monday, but by Tuesday they had closed at their July 2025 levels (d2), erasing the momentum from the rebound. The surge was attributed to a positive reaction to Huang's comeback, though investors reportedly continued selling over concerns that AI money is too expensive, demand too tenuous, and politics too uncertain. Monday marked the largest single-day value creation in market history as Nvidia added $1 trillion (q3). In remarks to employees on Tuesday, Huang said he has no plans to change structural weaknesses—including a lack of succession planning—that contributed to a recent corporate governance crisis.
items.title: Nvidia's Stock Rally After Jensen Huang's Return Fades

items.summary: Anthropic shares fell below their $83-a-share IPO price on Tuesday, sliding toward the original target of $78 a share. The listing was reportedly six times oversubscribed. Jay Ritter, described as academia's godfather of IPO research, explained that investors in anticipated deals often inflate their orders assuming they'll be cut back, noting this is not the same as actual desire to own the stock and that pension funds tend to be excluded from allocations entirely. Investment banks are said to steer shares toward favored hedge-fund clients likely to sell into an IPO pop; Anthropic shares opened last week above $111, a first-trade gain of 34%. The article notes supply and demand now appear to be fighting it out, which is harder for a $1 trillion-plus company with a murky path to profitability. SpaceX was cited as another example whose shares are down 22% since its IPO. Ritter reportedly placed an order in his Schwab account for 3,000 shares but received only 51.
items.title: Anthropic Stock Falls Below IPO Price Amid Alleged Allocation Gamesmanship

items.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang returned as chief executive on Monday after the company received input from senior U.S. government officials, including a call from President Donald Trump, that his reinstatement posed no national security risk; however, this development has not eased scrutiny over allegations that Nvidia's advanced GPUs were smuggled into China by Singapore-based data center operator Megaspeed in violation of U.S. export rules. The central question for investigators is what Nvidia knew about where the chips ended up and whether Huang's relationship with a Megaspeed executive gave the company reason to doubt Megaspeed's assurances, according to TechCrunch reporting citing export-control attorneys. The U.S. government opened an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 and requested information from Nvidia about its billions of dollars in sales to the company, concerned that chips bought for data center projects in Malaysia were being diverted to China; Singapore also began investigating similar allegations in 2025, while Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing. On Monday, the U.S. government added Megaspeed and its affiliates to a list of companies restricted from U.S. trade due to national security concerns, issued new rules barring large data centers that purchase U.S. chips from serving customers in China and other nations seen as problematic by the U.S. government, and Nvidia said it would stop selling licensed chips to China while laying out plans to hire its first compliance officer and create a new board committee focused on export controls. The Wall Street Journal reported that Alice Huang and her husband Kang Wei were part of a network of businesses that funneled chips to a company in Shanghai, with Kang reportedly introducing his wife to Jensen Huang, whom he had known for a decade; the concern Nvidia's board faced when it decided to oust Huang was that he knew more about what Megaspeed was doing with Nvidia's products than was reflected in any of the compliance statements. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Tuesday that Nvidia is 'a good corporate citizen' and suggested it is not a target of an investigation, but declined to answer questions about the government's ongoing investigation into Megaspeed; meanwhile, Nvidia faces investigations by California Attorney General Rob Bonta and reportedly the Securities and Exchange Commission over its corporate disclosures, with short sellers complaining about the company's decision to stop breaking out its exports to Singapore in financial filings after journalists raised concerns about chip diversion. Members of Congress from both parties want answers from Nvidia, including three House committees that will privately interview Huang and Nvidia top lawyer Tim Teter next week, citing alarm about China and some questioning the White House's role in Huang's return; Senate Banking Committee ranking member Elizabeth Warren said on Tuesday that 'Mr. Huang, Nvidia executives, and the company's board still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls' and that the Trump Administration needs to explain what input was given by senior officials to support his reinstatement.
items.title: Jensen Huang's Nvidia Return Amid Ongoing Megaspeed Chip Diversion Scrutiny

items.summary:
As an exceptionally strong El Niño intensifies in the equatorial Pacific, the Amazon rainforest faces a dangerous combination of scorching temperatures and reduced rainfall. According to figures released by the Amazon Cooperation Treaty Organization (ACTO), 73% of the Amazon basin experienced below-average rainfall in October, while fire hotspots surged 82.6% from a year earlier to nearly 24,000 across the region. Temperatures averaged 1.32 degrees Celsius above normal during that period.

NASA reported that El Niño-associated drought contributed to a sharp increase in forest fires across parts of the Brazilian Amazon since September, with thick smoke blanketing Manaus and Santarém and forcing school closures amid hazardous air pollution. NOAA said Thursday that sea-surface temperatures had reached 2.5 degrees Celsius above average, with about a 60% chance the current El Niño would surpass events dating back to 1950.

Paul Roundy, professor of atmospheric sciences at the University of Albany in New York, told Anadolu Agency that an El Niño of this strength could trigger reduced rainfall, hotter temperatures and drier conditions across parts of the Amazon biome. He cautioned it remains difficult to separate climate change's influence from natural variability in any single event.

Forecasters expect El Niño to remain exceptionally strong through end of 2026 into early 2027 as the rainy season begins, potentially disrupting seasonal rainfall and prolonging drought conditions. Roundy explained that subsidence—descending air over regions like the Amazon—compresses and warms air while lowering humidity, increasing wildfire risk.

El Niño's global impacts are already evident elsewhere. In Indonesia, approximately 1.9 million hectares burned during an exceptionally hot dry fire season between August and October, exposing about 12.5 million people to hazardous haze. A World Weather Attribution study found El Niño reduced seasonal rainfall in affected regions by about 50% and made short periods of extreme fire weather roughly five times more likely.

In Ecuador, authorities recorded 1,500 rain-related incidents across all 24 provinces between late August and Nov. 14 amid widespread flooding and landslides. Hurricane Polo rapidly intensified into a Category 5 storm over the eastern Pacific before striking Mexico and bringing heavy rainfall to parts of southwestern United States; an October World Weather Attribution study found El Niño made conditions favorable for its potential intensity about 14 times more likely, though human-caused climate change had even greater influence.

Historical precedents underscore concern: MAAP data show the 2015 "Godzilla El Niño" was followed by a record-breaking fire season in 2016 with 1.76 million hectares (4.3 million acres) of primary rainforest burned, and a strong late-2023 El Niño preceded extreme drought causing 2.8 million hectares of forest loss across the Amazon in 2024. The pattern has raised particular concerns about the 2027 fire season.

Despite uncertainty, Roundy said there is enough confidence in forecasts that governments and populations still have time to prepare for further water shortages and fires. In Peru's remote Purus region along Brazil's eastern border, Huni Kuin Indigenous leader Nolasco Torres told Anadolu his village of Balta fears extreme drought next year could reduce the Curanja River to an unnavigable stream.
items.title: Severe El Niño Threatens Amazon Rainforest With Drought and Fire Risk

items.summary: Amazon Global Selling has crossed $27 billion in cumulative exports from India, marking a milestone that underscores the growing role of e-commerce in the country's global trade ambitions. The government is targeting $200–300 billion in e-commerce exports by 2030, which could open significant opportunities for Indian businesses in international markets.
items.title: Amazon Global Selling Crosses $27 Billion in Indian Exports

items.summary: Federal Reserve Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle W. Bowman addressed an ASBA–BCBS–FSI High-Level Meeting on banking supervision, delivered via pre-recorded video from Brasília, Brazil, on November 25, 2026 (d1). She outlined three interrelated priorities: learning the right lessons from supervisory failures, modernizing regulatory and supervisory frameworks, and strengthening cooperation among supervisors in the Americas. Bowman drew on Silicon Valley Bank's March 2023 failure (d2) as a case study of how supervision failed to translate identified risks into timely action; an independent review she initiated found that between 2019 and March 2023 supervisors cited 54 supervisory matters requiring attention (q5), yet none required the bank to shorten its securities portfolio maturity or restructure its held-to-maturity book. She emphasized that supervision should be measured by whether material risks are identified, mitigated, and remediated in time rather than by examination counts, findings issued, or reports produced. On modernization, Bowman described Federal Reserve efforts including an Updated Statement of Supervisory Operating Principles (press release dated November 18, 2025; d11) that refocuses supervision on material risks with clearer expectations and judgment over procedural requirements, a reorganization clarifying decisionmaking authority through regional leadership while preserving local examination teams, and frameworks adapted to innovation. She noted the FSB released eight high-level modernization principles in October 2026 (d16), which she chairs for its Standing Committee on Supervisory and Regulatory Cooperation, cautioning that post-failure analyses should be tested against evidence before shaping global standards. Bowman also stressed regional cooperation among interconnected banking systems across the Americas—citing trade finance, cross-border lending, payments, remittances, money laundering threats, and shared technology questions—and identified ASBA as a valuable forum to deepen supervisory exchanges, build leadership capabilities, cooperate on emerging technologies, strengthen crisis preparedness relationships, and inform international standards.
items.title: Bowman Outlines a Shared Agenda for Modernizing Banking Supervision in the Americas

items.summary: Business Today Television aired a live conversation with Srinidhi Kalvapudi, Head of Amazon Global Selling India, exploring how Indian small businesses are exporting Made-in-India products globally. According to the program's framing, Indian e-commerce exports have surged past $27 billion (q2), and there is a stated roadmap for these figures to reach $80 billion by 2030 (q3, d4). The discussion highlighted that entrepreneurs from manufacturing clusters such as Erode, Moradabad, and Bhadohi are building global brands across more than 200 countries (q5), with health and beauty alongside home textiles cited as among the fastest-growing export categories. It was also reported that these products reach customers on over 18 Amazon marketplaces (q6). The segment framed Indian e-commerce exports at over 1 billion Made-in-India units sold worldwide (q1) and explored how MSMEs can leverage AI tools, global logistics, and overseas demand to expand their international trade.
items.title: Amazon Global Selling India Discusses Indian E-Commerce Export Growth

items.summary: Global markets fell on Wednesday amid a broad selloff of riskier assets after the Trump administration proposed sweeping new tariffs on major trading partners. US technology shares led declines amid concerns about inflation and a hawkish Federal Reserve, while Treasury prices jumped as investors sought safe-haven assets. MSCI's global stocks index fell 2.35 per cent (q1), while Nvidia shed more than 8 per cent (q2). The Nasdaq was down 3.9 per cent (q3), the S&P 500 down 2.7 per cent (q5) and the Dow down 1.7 per cent (q6). The selloff extended beyond US markets, with Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan down 2.28 per cent (q7) and emerging market stocks falling 3.23 per cent (q8), while the pan-European STOXX 600 fell 0.67 per cent (q10). Aneeka Gupta, an equity strategist at WisdomTree, said markets were contending with AI concerns alongside hawkish central banks and renewed tariffs that add volatility. European shares had traded higher earlier on gains in personal and household goods and retail stocks before reversing course. The broad-based selloff, combined with lower bond yields, weaker cryptocurrencies and falling industrial metals prices, signalled growing concern that escalating trade barriers could weigh on global growth and corporate earnings. ING analysts wrote that while the legal justification for tariffs keeps changing, US protectionism is becoming increasingly difficult to unwind, noting that an earlier Supreme Court ruling did not mark the end of the tariff wall. Nvidia gave up about half of its gains from earlier in the week, leaving the stock down about 14 per cent since Monday (q11), when CEO Jensen Huang's return sparked a 31.5 per cent rally (q12). US consumer confidence increased by more than expected in November to its highest level in nearly two years. The dollar index rose 0.15 per cent (q13) while the euro slipped 0.26 per cent to $1.0936 (q14, q15). Derek Halpenny of MUFG wrote that higher interest rates are creating challenges for investors and undermining confidence in the financing structures driving AI expansion. Euro zone government bond yields fell as the slide in US equities drove investors toward sovereign debt; Germany's benchmark 10-year Bund yield fell 4.73 basis points to 3.218 per cent from 3.266 per cent late on Tuesday (q16, q17, q18). Brent rose 2.19 per cent to $93.40 per barrel (q19, q20).
items.title: World stocks tumble as Trump tariffs rattle markets, AI rally fades

items.summary:
President Donald Trump said Tuesday he is open to pardoning reinstated Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang for any potential federal crimes, though he does not believe a pardon will be necessary. Speaking in an interview with the New York Post published Tuesday, Trump said, "It's always an option, I guess, but I don't think it'll be necessary." He urged Huang to tell the truth and stated he did not think the CEO needed to invoke his Fifth Amendment rights, adding that he has found Huang to be "100% aboveboard" and a very smart person. Trump's pardon power extends only to offenses under federal law, not state law.

Huang is scheduled to sit for a private session with House committees on Dec. 1, then face a public Senate committee hearing on Dec. 3. Sen. John Kennedy, a Louisiana Republican, said Monday that he anticipates Huang will invoke his Fifth Amendment rights to avoid self-incrimination in criminal prosecution, according to CNBC.

Topics for the closed-door session include Jensen Huang's affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang—who is suspected of spying for China and who is not related to him—as well as the practices Nvidia uses to safeguard its information, according to Bloomberg. Three House committee chairs have said the reinstatement does not end their demands for answers on chip smuggling to China; they reported that Jensen Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter confirmed they will appear for transcribed interviews on Dec. 1 and Dec. 2.

Nvidia's board voted unanimously Monday to bring Huang back, less than two weeks after he resigned Nov. 12 amid reports of multiple affairs. U.S. officials suspect one of the women involved was relaying information to China's intelligence services, an allegation Beijing has dismissed.

Several Republican lawmakers criticized the reinstatement and Trump's role in it. On Truth Social, Trump wrote that acting Attorney General Todd Blanche confirmed the government has no evidence Huang engaged in unlawful conduct.
items.title: Trump Says Pardon for Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Is Possible

items.summary:
More than a year after the United Nations Convention against Cybercrime (UNCC) was signed in Hanoi, Vietnam, its implementation remains unsettled. During the January 2026 Session of the Ad Hoc Committee on the Rules of Procedure for the Conference of the States Parties, member states failed to reach consensus on draft rules—particularly Rules 16 and 17 concerning participation by non-governmental stakeholders—with a Mexico proposal reflected in the AHC Chair's consolidated draft forming the basis for continued negotiations. The disagreements concern observer accreditation duration, opportunities for civil society intervention, and restrictions on references to country-specific situations, which will determine whether civil society can contribute substantive expertise or only narrow procedural participation.

Following that session, informal deliberations continued with limited transparency for non-governmental stakeholders while governments advanced proposals for a possible supplementary protocol before the convention's implementation had been tested. The proposed offenses vary considerably in scope: China's draft covers terrorism, extortion, prohibited goods, online gambling, intellectual property, and intentional dissemination of false information using AI; Russia's is broader still, covering terrorism, extremism, public disorder, historical content offenses, trafficking, suicide inducement, personal-data offenses, criminal use of AI, plus a catch-all provision for other ICT-related unlawful acts causing substantial harm. Other proposals address online scams, fraud, cyber-extortion involving cryptocurrency affecting communities in Africa and Asia, technology-facilitated violence against women and children (raised by Brazil), online incitement, trafficking, and illicit digital platform activity.

Several governments have called for restraint: the European Union supported evidence-based assessment of needs and gaps with clearly defined offenses; Norway cautioned against creating offenses where ICT use does not materially change conduct or existing instruments already address it; the United Kingdom proposed a two-part assessment of whether the convention is insufficient and whether international frameworks leave a genuine gap; New Zealand argued emerging technologies alone do not justify additional obligations. The article notes these positions point to a sequencing problem, since states already have tools to address cyber-enabled crime.

On investigative powers, Russia's draft would extend electronic surveillance, online undercover operations, cross-border searches at foreign authority request, and service-provider assistance; Algeria proposed permanent points of contact, secure evidence exchange, joint investigations, and faster preservation procedures. Ecuador, Sierra Leone, and the EU emphasized legality, necessity, proportionality, data protection, independent oversight, dual criminality, judicial review, and protection against mass surveillance (Sierra Leone), while Mexico warned interception powers should not enable excessive control.

The article flags that a supplementary protocol arrives amid expanding domestic digital controls: Zambia's Cyber Security Act of 2025 and Cyber Crimes Act of 2025 introduced vague speech offenses like criminalizing false-information publication with broad interception powers, and Mexico's July 2025 reforms require biometric line registration while expanding access to geolocation and communications metadata without prior judicial authorization. The piece concludes that the convention's value depends on exercising its powers effectively, accountably, and with public scrutiny before further obligations are considered.
items.title: UN Cybercrime Convention Implementation Unsettled as Supplementary Protocol Proposals Advance

items.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump introduced fresh tariff proposals targeting 14 trading partners—including China, the European Union, Japan, and Vietnam—following an eight-month trade probe into excess industrial capacity (q1). Proposed rates could reach up to 40% for China if trade talks fail (q2), while a truce expiring in January would impose a lower 20% baseline cap that may stack with existing duties (q3); other partners face varied caps pending negotiations and public comment. The proposals come after the U.S. Supreme Court struck down broader tariffs imposed earlier, prompting live debate over economic and market impacts.
items.title: Trump Unveils New Tariff Proposals After Supreme Court Ruling

items.summary: Singapore trade finance firm Incomlend has applied to withdraw its lawsuit against iron ore trader Radiant World, according to a hearing schedule posted on the city-state's court website. The summons for withdrawal or discontinuance is listed for a Nov. 30 hearing and does not provide a reason for the move; neither Incomlend nor Radiant World immediately responded to requests for comment. Incomlend joined several creditors who filed legal action against Radiant World after some banks and counterparties stopped doing business with it amid allegations that it falsified invoices to secure financing. The firm's spokesperson denied wrongdoing, stating the trader conducts business "to the highest commercial and legal standards." According to Incomlend's Singapore court filings, the company provided Radiant World with over US$30 million (S$38.76 million) in credit earlier in 2026 underpinned by two invoices purportedly for sales to commodity giant Glencore, which Glencore later told it were not genuine. Separately, in September a Singapore High Court judge appointed KPMG as interim judicial managers of Radiant World's Singapore operating entity in a case brought by creditor Mizuho Bank; Judge Kristy Tan wrote there was enough initial evidence that Radiant World "is or is likely to become unable to pay its debts" to support the appointment.
items.title: Incomlend Files to Withdraw Lawsuit Against Radiant World

items.summary: Nasdaq-100 futures dropped about 3% while Dow Jones Industrial Average futures lost 635 points, or 1.3%, after the personal consumption expenditures price index accelerated to a 3.8% annual rate in October (rising 0.3% for the month), with core PCE—which excludes food and energy—climbing 3.3% year over year above a Dow Jones forecast, according to CNBC. S&P 500 futures fell about 2%, and Nasdaq-100 futures also shed roughly 3%. Individual technology stocks declined sharply: Anthropic stock fell 4%, Oracle stock dropped about 6%, Alphabet stock shed 4%, and the State Street Technology Select Sector ETF (XLK) was down by over 3%.
items.title: Stock Futures Tumble as Nvidia Leads an AI Sell-off and Inflation Data Shows Prices Picking Up

items.summary: Days after CEO Satya Nadella apologized for a major outage that disrupted Outlook and other Microsoft 365 services worldwide, the company declared its highest-priority “Code Red” initiative to overhaul engineering, incident response, and service recovery processes, according to internal memos reviewed by Reuters. The disruption followed the November 12-13 outage that affected governments, businesses, and consumers across multiple countries including Australia, Japan, and the United States.
items.title: Microsoft Declares 'Code Red' After Global Outlook Outage

items.summary: In a letter to the forum titled 'Help kitchens make practical use of alternative food sources,' Madan Kishor, who describes himself as working in hospitality and training, welcomed the collaboration announced by CapitaLand Investment and the Restaurant Association of Singapore aimed at helping food and beverage operators diversify their food sources. He argued that while access to an additional supplier is a useful starting point, turning such options into operationally ready choices requires preparation at the outlet level. Kishor proposed that operators conduct simple exercises in which they select key ingredients, test alternatives within their dishes, and document any adjustments needed to preparation, portion sizes, and cooking methods. He further suggested that industry partners could support smaller operators through joint product trials or practical demonstrations where such resources are not already available. According to the letter, these efforts should aim to provide operators with workable options suited to their menus, budgets, and customers.
items.title: Reader Suggests Practical Steps for Using Alternative Food Sources in Singapore Kitchens

items.summary: In a letter responding to Pang Chong Liu's Nov. 11 submission on workplace support for employees with disabilities, SG Enable welcomed the refreshed Enabling Mark framework's emphasis on sustained employment and endorsed his suggestion of a simple handover checklist—particularly useful for smaller firms lacking dedicated HR teams—which SG Enable will explore as it develops resources for small and medium-sized enterprises. The organization noted that inclusive employers work with SG Enable and its partners to arrange workplace accommodations, designate points of contact, and review arrangements regularly with job coaches, ideally incorporating these into the supervisor's handover so employees continue receiving needed support during transitions; employees and employers may also approach SG Enable directly for guidance on managing such changes. Aligning with recommendations from the Taskforce on Assurance for Families with Persons with Disabilities to strengthen employment retention and career-building support, SG Enable announced that its Employment Support Office will offer career and skills advisory services beginning in the second half of 2027, and starting in 2028 it will extend job-support duration for persons with higher work support needs in open employment while continuing assistance whenever workplace challenges arise. The letter was signed by Edward Chew, Senior Director of SG Enable's Employment and Lifelong Learning Group.
items.title: SG Enable to Expand Support for Employees with Disabilities Through Workplace Transitions

items.summary: The United States has proposed a 25 percent tariff on Indian goods following Section 301 investigations into unfair trade and labour conditions across 17 countries. Implementation is likely delayed until early next year after a public comment period, with the proposal serving as a benchmark for India to negotiate market access and finalize trade agreement terms.
items.title: US Proposes 25 Percent Tariff on India After Trade Probe

items.summary: The United States proposed fresh tariffs of up to 25% on Indian products Wednesday, following a Section 301 investigation launched in March into alleged excess production. The US Office of the Trade Representative said these duties would replace rather than be added to India's existing 10% tariff and would fall to 17% if New Delhi and Washington sign a formal trade agreement. The proposed levies target goods from 13 other economies, including China and the European Union; for China they add a new 20% duty on top of the 25% imposed in 2018 over forced technology transfers, bringing total tariffs to 45%, while Vietnam would face the highest rate at 35%. The remaining countries targeted are Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam. Under Section 301 of the 1974 Trade Act, Washington may investigate foreign trade practices it considers discriminatory to US commerce; the new tariffs would be subject to a public comment period before taking effect.
items.title: US Proposes Tariffs of Up to 25% on India and 13 Other Trade Partners

items.summary: The United States has proposed import tariffs of up to 25 percent on goods from India, following an investigation into alleged trade violations and manufacturing excess. The proposal comes as talks between the two countries continue ahead of the G20 Summit, with certain exemptions noted in the broadcast by reporter Gaurav Sawant. Separately, political disputes are rising within India: debates over seat-sharing between the Samajwadi Party and Congress have surfaced ahead of 2027 Uttar Pradesh elections amid coalition tensions, while legal issues emerge in Tamil Nadu concerning a Supreme Court order about the Karthigai Deepam festival, prompting explanations from the state Governor, an apology from the Madurai Collector for the administration's stance, and condemnation by the BJP.
items.title: US Proposes Tariffs on Indian Goods Amid Trade Dispute

items.summary: The Trump administration has proposed new tariffs on some goods from 14 major trading partners—China, Bangladesh, Cambodia, the EU, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam—to curb what it says is excess factory output fuelled by subsidies and other trade barriers that disadvantage US manufacturers. The proposal follows an eight-month Section 301 investigation by the Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) targeting excess capacity in 16 trading partners; USTR found practices unreasonable in 14 of those economies, while investigations into Mexico and Norway remain pending with both excluded from the current proposal. Public comments are due by January 5, 2027, hearings begin January 25, and no effective date has been set. The White House announced plans to impose 15% tariffs on EU goods above existing most-favoured-nation duties, with an option of up to 20% if ongoing talks are found unsatisfactory; some Section 232-covered products such as cars, steel and aluminium would be exempted. For China the USTR proposes rates of up to 20%, deducting any existing forced-labour tariff, up to 10% on some products with others exempted, and a possible rate of up to 40% if talks fail. The administration says low-priced imports have contributed to the US goods trade deficit, which reached $1.24 trillion (€1.13tn) in 2025.
items.title: US Proposes New Tariffs on Goods From 14 Trading Partners Including the EU

items.summary: US Trade Representative announced a new suite of tariffs targeting more than a dozen major trading partners, including China, Bangladesh, Cambodia, the European Union, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam — while Australia is not affected. The duties stem from an Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) investigation into excess industrial capacity under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which defines such capacity as a market able to produce more goods than demand, leading to overproduction and persistent trade surpluses. For some Chinese goods, the new 20 per cent tariff (q2) stacks on top of existing import taxes for a total rate of 45 per cent (q3), while Vietnam faces a 20 per cent tariff (q4). Tariffs for other trading partners range from 10 to 18 per cent (q5, q6). Brazil was also singled out after stalled trade talks with a new 10 per cent tariff on aircraft exports affecting Embraer, plus increased duties on raw and refined sugar (q7). The Trump administration previously identified China as the biggest source of excess industrial capacity. These tariffs will stack on top of some existing rates from earlier in Mr Trump's second term, though many are capped at lower levels due to prior deals with individual countries. On legal grounds, a Reuters/Ipsos opinion poll conducted after recent midterm elections showed 62 per cent of respondents would support efforts to repeal the tariffs (q11). Separately, SCOTUS struck down Mr Trump's February national-emergency tariff authority in February but left other tariffs implemented under different legislation intact.
items.title: Trump Unveils New Tariffs on More Than a Dozen Trading Partners

visual.alt: Bar chart. China (new) 20 %; Total China (stacked) 45 %; Vietnam 20 %.

items.summary: The Trump administration announced proposed tariffs under a new eight-month investigation into alleged excess manufacturing capacity and industrial subsidies, covering 14 major trading partners including India, China, Japan and the European Union. The Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR) released the proposals on November 25; they are not final and will undergo a public consultation process followed by a hearing before implementation, which could be pushed to January 2027.
items.title: US Proposes Section 301 Tariffs on India, China and 12 Other Economies

items.summary: Prime Minister Narendra Modi reportedly asked his ministers to complete preparations for the next session of Parliament before December 15 and avoid foreign travel in the run-up, according to sources cited by news agency PTI. The matter was discussed at Wednesday's Cabinet meeting chaired by Modi, who suggested convening the session before that date while instructing ministries to ensure readiness; however, the Cabinet Committee on Parliamentary Affairs will take the final call on the commencement date and duration of the sitting. As of Wednesday night, the Monsoon Session remained unprorogued more than 100 days after both Houses were adjourned indefinitely on August 13.
items.title: Modi Asks Ministers to Stay Ready; Parliament Session Likely Before December 15

items.summary: US-listed exchange-traded funds (ETFs) investing in Bitcoin are heading for the worst month of outflows since their 2024 debut, driven by a persistent sell-off in the world's largest cryptocurrency. A net US$4.71 billion (S$6 billion) has been withdrawn from these funds in November so far, according to data compiled by Bloomberg through Nov 23. BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust, the largest fund holding the token, has suffered about US$4 billion of redemptions in November, also putting it on course for its worst monthly outflow. The exodus comes as Bitcoin tumbles below US$60,000 and heads for its worst monthly performance since June 2022, when a string of corporate failures triggered a broader crypto market meltdown. The token has dropped about 23% in November and was trading around US$59,200 as at 1pm on Nov 25 in Singapore, down about 1% in the Asia session.
items.title: Bitcoin ETFs Face Worst Monthly Outflows as Bitcoin Falls Below $60,000

visual.alt: Bar chart. November 2024 (ETF net outflow (US$)) 23 %; November 2024 (Bitcoin daily change in Asia session (Nov 25)) 1 %.

items.summary: The United States proposed a tariff of up to 25 per cent on Indian goods Wednesday following a months-long investigation into what Washington calls structural excess capacity across 16 major economies. According to a list released by the US Trade Representative (USTR), the rate would fall to 17 per cent if New Delhi signs an interim trade deal with Washington; at that level, most Indian goods would see a rise of seven percentage points over current duties. The proposed duty will not be added to the existing 10 per cent tariff on Indian exporters imposed since July under a separate forced-labour investigation—importers instead pay whichever rate is higher—and it also will not stack onto Section 232 national-security duties, with energy products, food, critical minerals, fertilisers and certain semiconductors and pharmaceuticals exempt. Public hearings are expected to begin soon, though the tariffs are unlikely to take effect before January.
items.title: US Proposes Up to 25% 'Excess Capacity' Tariff on India, 17% If Trade Deal Signed

items.summary: Beijing urged the United States on Wednesday to uphold stable trade relations after media reports indicated Washington was planning new tariffs affecting China, the European Union, Japan and South Korea. Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said tariff wars are not in anyone's interest and that the two economies should resolve issues through consultation rather than conflict. He dismissed accusations of overcapacity as a false premise used to justify political manipulation, calling for continued implementation of the consensus reached by US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. The reports come amid an ongoing trade dispute dating back to tariffs imposed after Trump's second term began last year, which escalated at one point to duties as high as 145%. A ceasefire struck between Trump and Xi in October 2025 is due to expire in January following a two-month extension agreed in September. The two leaders met recently at an APEC summit in Shenzhen ahead of a trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin, where Xi praised China's improved ties with the United States and called for cooperation on artificial intelligence.
items.title: China Pushes Back Against Reported US Tariff Plans

items.summary: The United States has proposed raising its base tariff on Indian goods from 18% to 25%, reversing an earlier decision to cut the rate after waiving a separate 25% punitive duty tied to India's purchases of Russian oil. According to Reuters, the USTR office put forward this proposal as part of a broader set of proposed rates covering multiple countries following an eight-month probe into alleged unfair trade practices by 16 nations; China would face a higher base tariff of 40%, Vietnam 35%, and EU member states, Japan, Switzerland, Singapore and Bangladesh up to 20%. The USTR stated the measures reflect its reciprocal-trade framework and warned that tariffs could rise further if negotiations break down. India's proposed rate is lower than China's because Washington has said New Delhi would pay only 17% base tariff if it signs a Bilateral Trade Agreement, prompting analysts to speculate the proposal may be used as leverage over the farm sector, which remains an unresolved sticking point in talks between Foreign Minister S Jaishankar and Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal. The USTR cited evidence of structural excess capacity in Indian sectors such as solar modules—where current manufacturing is nearly triple annual domestic demand—as well as petrochemicals and steel. Separately, the text notes that India's bilateral trade surplus with the United States was $58 billion in 2025, while India-China trade reached $155.6 billion in 2025 with a record seven-month deficit of $83 billion; analysts warn that any US-China concessions could increase competition and pressure Indian exports to the US and EU.
items.title: US Proposes Raising Base Tariff on Indian Goods to 25% Amid US-India Trade Talks

visual.alt: Bar chart. India 25 %; China 40 %.

items.summary: The United States has proposed a 17% tariff on Indian goods under a new trade framework unveiled by President Donald Trump's administration, placing India among 14 economies targeted by Washington in its effort to address what it describes as excess manufacturing capacity and production among major trading partners (q2: '14 economies'). According to the Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR), tariffs on Indian exports could be as high as 25% under this framework, though that rate would fall back to 17% if New Delhi reaches a trade agreement with Washington (q3: '25 per cent', q4: '17 per cent'). The proposal is part of a broader package covering several economies, including China, the European Union, Japan, South Korea, Vietnam and Bangladesh. It follows an investigation launched by the USTR in March to examine whether foreign governments were maintaining manufacturing capacity and production levels that exceed actual market demand, resulting in oversupply and distortions in global trade; US officials argue such practices depress prices and undermine domestic manufacturing industries.
items.title: US Proposes Tariffs on India Under New Excess Capacity Trade Framework

items.summary: The United States has proposed imposing tariffs of up to 25% on Indian goods following an investigation into what Washington describes as 'structural excess capacity' in major economies. However, this rate could be reduced to 17% if India reaches a trade agreement with the US (q1: 25%, q2: 17%). According to reports from the Office of the US Trade Representative's list released Wednesday, the proposed 17% rate is lower than the 18% agreed upon under an interim trade deal framework in February (q3: 17%, q4: 18%). A senior US trade official said the proposed duties would not be added to the existing 10% tariff imposed on Indian exporters under a separate investigation into forced labour; importers would instead pay whichever rate is higher (q11: 10%). The tariffs are unlikely to come into effect before January, as public hearings and consultations remain pending. India and the US have yet to finalise their interim trade agreement, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi expected to meet President Donald Trump at next month's G20 summit in Florida.
items.title: US Proposes Tariffs of Up to 25% on Indian Goods, With Possible Reduction

items.summary: On November 23, Ford Motor Company announced a minority stake in US startup Revolution Space through its Industrial Platform LLC subsidiary for an undisclosed sum. The automaker said it will apply its manufacturing experience to help industrialize Revolution's next-generation spacecraft at scale and support proliferated constellations, with Chief Strategy Officer Marin Gjaja noting that building complex products in large volumes is what the growing satellite market requires. Ford cited a press statement estimating the global space economy at about $600 billion today versus roughly $1.8 trillion by 2035, and attributed Future Market Insights' estimate of the global satellite manufacturing market rising from around $22–$26 billion currently to between $87 billion and $114 billion by 2035 as a driver of that growth. Ford listed communications, Earth observation, navigation, space domain awareness, satellite servicing, and scientific and deep-space missions among its areas of interest. Revolution Space's board is chaired by former NASA administrator Daniel Goldin, with former astronaut Paul W. Richards serving as Chief Engineer and Chief Strategy Officer; the company was selected for DARPA's LASSO program in 2025 to build a spacecraft that maps lunar regions containing more than 5% water concentration. Revolution also reported receiving awards from the Defense Innovation Unit's Advanced Capabilities & Demonstration Missions program and the Department of Defense's Accelerate the Procurement and Fielding of Innovative Technologies program in 2024, plus an agreement with NASA to collaborate on space technology. Separately, a November 24 Wall Street Journal report indicated Ford is among automakers being enlisted by the Pentagon to help supply drones through actuators, engines, sensors, lidar and other components; CleanTechnica attributed reports that Ford has had discussions with the Pentagon about its Revolution Space investment and military vehicle manufacturing to Detroit Free Press spokesperson David Tovar. The article also noted a separate Tesla–SpaceX merger discussion involving Elon Musk.
items.title: Ford Takes Minority Stake in Revolution Space, Joining Automakers Entering the Space Race

items.summary: The article reports a benchmark in which an automated agent tuned the serving of the newly released open-source model Inkling 2 Mini (~26B total parameters, ~3B active per token, multimodal inputs, and a 1M-token context window) on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 (96 GB), behind both Hugging Face Jobs and an Inference Endpoint. The authors describe the model's unusual looped Mixture-of-Experts architecture—24 physical layers with the middle 12 run three times so each token passes through 48 layers—and note that published serving recipes target NVIDIA B200/GB300 GPUs, leaving out sm120 cards like the RTX PRO 6000. The agent ran experiments for an afternoon across 46 valid benchmark runs using a fixed protocol (measure hardware and ceilings first; change one variable at a time with bracketing control runs; log every run including regressions; pass long-context, concurrency, and greedy-equivalence checks). Single-user decode speed rose from 136 to 190.6 tok/s (+40%), ahead of the community SGLang + DSpark benchmark (167.7 tok/s) on LocalMaxxing for the same GPU, while 8-user aggregate throughput went from ~570 to 716 tok/s (+26%) using vLLM nightly with DSpark speculative decoding; greedy outputs were byte-identical with and without speculation, long-context needle retrieval passed 3/3 up to 250K tokens, and the winning config is now running as an Inference Endpoint from a pinned image digest. All logs, scripts, and raw measurements are in NielsRogge/inkling-2-mini-hillclimb.
items.title: Hill-climbing Inkling 2 Mini inference on one RTX PRO 6000

items.summary: In early 1935, the Central Red Army faced pursuit by Kuomintang forces during the Long March and turned a difficult position into a strategic breakthrough through four crossings of the Chishui River in southwest China. The operations began after a January 1935 battle at Qinggangpo in Zunyi, Guizhou Province, that left more than 3,000 soldiers dead or wounded (q3), exposing the need to regroup and change approach. According to Mpaphi Kenosi, Botswana's defense attaché to China,
items.title: Foreign Defense Attachés Study the Red Army's Four Crossings of the Chishui River

items.summary: On November 25, 2026, China launched the crewed Shenzhou-24 mission from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China. The spacecraft carried Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo and Wu Yi alongside Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, marking the first time a foreign astronaut has joined a crewed flight to China's space station. Pakistan's Minister for Planning, Development and Special Initiatives, Ahsan Iqbal Chaudhary, who was at the launch site, expressed hope that the mission would pave the way for greater cooperation between the two countries and thanked China's leadership, scientists and engineers for their support; when asked whether Pakistan could one day send astronauts into space independently, he said "Certainly that day will come." The flight drew a wave of supportive messages on social media ahead of launch. Chinese Ambassador to the United States Xie Feng congratulated Ali in a post on X, writing: "The universe has no borders. Together, let's go further." Saif Nasser, media attaché at the Saudi Embassy in Islamabad, described the mission as "a proud moment for Pakistan" and said it would inspire many young Pakistanis. Turkish broadcaster TRT World highlighted that Ali was set to become the first foreign astronaut aboard China's space station, carrying "the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis." Blaine Curcio, founder of Hong Kong-based Orbital Gateway Consulting, told Reuters that the flight would bring Pakistan "prestige, important science and technology know-how, and a level of deeper collaboration and diplomatic goodwill with China." Experts interviewed by Nature also pointed to broader implications: Wajiha Iqbal, a lunar scientist at the University of Münster in Germany, called the mission "a huge step" for Pakistan's space ambitions, saying the partnership would enable scientific research in space; Yuxuan Jia, a China foreign policy researcher at the Center for China and Globalization, said China's expanding space capabilities allow it to offer international partners opportunities that few countries can provide on their own. As the crew begins its mission aboard China's space station, the flight marks a new step in international cooperation in China's space program and opens up further opportunities for collaboration in space science and exploration.
items.title: China Launches Shenzhou-24 With Pakistani Astronaut Aboard Space Station

items.summary: The Shenzhou-24 crew, comprising Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo and Wu Yi along with Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, entered China's Tiangong space station on Wednesday after their spacecraft successfully docked at 11:56 a.m. Beijing Time, according to the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA). The automated rendezvous and docking occurred over approximately 3.5 hours as the ship connected with the front port of the core module Tianhe. The crew had launched atop a Long March-2F carrier rocket at 8:18 a.m. Beijing Time from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China earlier that day, per CMSA. Upon arrival, the Shenzhou-23 crew members who were already aboard welcomed the new arrivals, and all six astronauts took a group photo on November 25, 2026.
items.title: Shenzhou-24 Crew Docks with and Enters China Space Station

items.summary: Jessica Durdu, a foreign affairs specialist with a PhD in law and special commentator for CGTN, published an opinion piece arguing that technology companies should not exclude talent based on identity. The article uses Anthropic's initial public offering as its central example, noting the company rang the opening bell at Nasdaq on November 19 to symbolize growing tech influence over global economy and competitiveness while raising questions about institutional inclusiveness in AI development. Durdu contends that although governments and corporations have legitimate responsibilities to protect sensitive technologies, intellectual property, and critical infrastructure during intensifying geopolitical competition, security considerations should be based on evidence rather than perceptions of nationality, ethnicity, or cultural background. The piece references the February 2022 termination of the US Department of Justice's China Initiative as an illustration that national security and equal opportunity need not conflict, with the department subsequently adopting a broader strategy for countering nation-state threats. Durdu argues identity-based barriers often emerge through informal networks in Silicon Valley's entrepreneurial ecosystem built on prestigious universities, previous employment, and professional communities, which can become mechanisms of institutional exclusion when access to strategic opportunities depends excessively on personal connections. The article cites the appointments of India-born Satya Nadella as Microsoft CEO and Sundar Pichai as Google CEO as examples demonstrating how internationally diverse talent provides strategic leadership rather than merely technical expertise. Durdu also references a June 2026 study by the National Foundation for American Policy finding that nearly one-quarter of US billion-dollar startups had at least one founder who initially entered the country as an international student, illustrating the economic value of international talent given opportunities to lead and make strategic decisions. The commentary asserts AI inclusive decision-making carries significance beyond corporate performance because AI systems increasingly operate across societies with different languages, cultural traditions, regulatory frameworks, and socioeconomic conditions where diverse professionals can contribute perspectives on algorithmic fairness, consumer expectations, and social implications of deployment. Durdu concludes that the future competitiveness of technology companies depends not only on computational power, financial resources, or intellectual property but also on cultivating institutional environments free from identity-based limitations, urging China, the United States, and other emerging tech centers to balance legitimate national interests with the international character of scientific advancement while recognizing talent as an indispensable partner rather than merely an instrument of technological production.
items.title: CGTN Commentator Argues Tech Giants Should Not Restrict Talent by Identity

items.summary: Discount retailer Poundland has collapsed into administration after its owners failed to secure a buyer to keep the business running. The company formally entered administration on Wednesday afternoon, just weeks before Christmas, following last-minute rescue talks with several bidders that reached no transaction. Poundland's boss filed for administration and appointed consultancy Alix Partners to oversee the process; administrators said they would look at all options including selling the business or its assets in whole or part, with some stores likely sold off to rival retailers. During the process, shops and distribution centres will remain open and continue trading.
items.title: Poundland Collapses Into Administration, Putting 11,000 Jobs at Risk

items.summary: At 10 a.m. ET, military explosives experts detonated degraded lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, sending a plume into the air that quickly dissipated. The controlled detonation was deemed necessary because decades-old stored material had partially crystallized and become increasingly sensitive to friction, shock, and cold winter temperatures, creating what officials described as a growing risk of spontaneous, uncontrolled explosion. Ahead of the operation, authorities warned that toxic lead dust could travel up to 100 miles from Iowa into parts of Missouri (q1), prompting evacuations of residents in and around Middletown; FEMA urged those who did not evacuate to shelter in place until an all-clear was issued. A court cleared the way for the detonation earlier this month despite concerns about health and environmental impacts, and the CDC activated an emergency response to support public-health communication.
items.title: US Army Detonates Degraded Lead Azide at Iowa Ammunition Plant

items.summary: COP31 closed without agreement on the proposed "Antalya pact," which was rejected by at least 32 countries including the EU, UK and some climate-vulnerable nations after talks overran by two days. Carbon Brief compiled global media reactions showing divergent views: many outlets called it a failure while noting that no formal cover decision was adopted even though agreement on other decisions was reached. Blame for the perceived collapse fell unevenly—oil-rich nations were widely blamed, with reports citing pressure from Russia and Saudi Arabia over omitting fossil-fuel language; developed countries faced criticism for blocking the pact and climate finance; developing nations emphasized equity, historical responsibility and finance; and China was portrayed by state media as a constructive participant. Australia's presidency drew specific scrutiny: an editorial in The Australian criticized president Chris Bowen over his handling of competing interests amid Australia's $150m investment in the conference (attributed to that outlet). Reform calls emerged widely, including from the European Commission drawing up plans to overhaul the UN climate summit process because a single country can block agreement among nearly 200 parties. Some outlets framed COP31 as sending a positive signal: Bloomberg reported more than 100 governments led by the EU opposed the final declaration that omitted any reference to transitioning away from fossil fuels.
items.title: Media Reactions to COP31's Rejected 'Antalya Pact'

items.summary: Director David Fincher, 64, took center stage at the London European premiere of The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth on Monday night while Quentin Tarantino and Brad Pitt were unavailable. The film follows stuntman Cliff Booth in a fading Los Angeles during 1977, around the release of Star Wars (d1). Fincher's version arrives in theaters Wednesday before becoming available on Netflix, marking the end of his seven-year relationship with the streaming platform that financed this promotional trip.
items.title: David Fincher Discusses 'The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth' at European Premiere

items.summary: A new documentary, The Slightest Touch, premiering on HBO Max on Wednesday, November 25, chronicles the friendship between Hollywood actor Colin Farrell and Irish woman Emma Fogarty. It follows the months leading up to an October 2024 Dublin Marathon that the pair planned to complete together — one kilometer for each decade of Fogarty's life (The Slightest Touch). The film runs about 90 minutes and centers on their friendship as well as Fogarty, now 42, who has epidermolysis bullosa. Farrell, a 50-year-old actor known for protecting his private life, discusses addictions he overcame years ago and reflects on fatherhood after losing his own father in April 2025 (The Slightest Touch). Fogarty is described as the oldest living person in Ireland with the condition; today around 90% of her body is covered in wounds, and her leg was amputated due to cancer she has beaten twice. She turned 40 recently, an emotional milestone given that no one with her condition had reached age 50 (The Slightest Touch). Farrell met Fogarty about 15 years ago at a fundraising event for epidermolysis bullosa awareness; their relationship began with two or three emails a year and now includes WhatsApp messages, voice notes and video calls ending in 'I love you.' The documentary also shows his son James, born September 12, 2003 (The Slightest Touch). Fogarty is an ambassador for DEBRA Ireland and has helped raise more than $1.1 million for the cause supporting people with epidermolysis bullosa (The Slightest Touch). For its London premiere in October, HBO chartered a private jet to transport Fogarty because she cannot fly commercially; she shared on Instagram that it was 'a trip a lifetime,' noting her account has more than 17,000 followers. Farrell later told The Guardian he had no desire to revisit the documentary but would do it again for Emma's story.
items.title: Colin Farrell's Documentary 'The Slightest Touch' Premieres on HBO Max

items.summary: Governor Kathy Hochul signed legislation Wednesday imposing a five-year ban on the manufacture and sale of toys powered by AI chatbots, including talking stuffed animals, dolls, and robots that use the internet to converse with children. The measure prohibits dangerous chatbots disguised as toys from exposing children to inappropriate conversations or putting their privacy at risk; parents shopping for children's toys should not have to worry about such exposure, Hochul said. The governor described the legislation as deeply personal, noting it is her job to put New York families first as a mother and grandmother. An NBC News study found that the Pixie Paw toy, marketed to children as young as three, shared details about firing squads and massacres and explained gang rape; an NBC report also examined the Pixie Paw Smart Interactive Plush Cat. Attorney General Letitia James said AI chatbots in children's toys are exposing young people to inappropriate content and putting their mental health at risk, adding that her office would not hesitate to enforce this law and other measures to stop AI systems from doing harm. Officials pointed to Trouble in Toyland, a consumer watchdog report from the US Public Interest Research Group Education Fund (PIRG), which tested AI chatbot-enabled toys marketed to children as young as three that talked about sexually explicit topics, told kids where likely matches could be found at home, and acted upset when a child had to leave. Hochul said some toys had few or no parental controls, with safety limits weakening the longer conversations continued; additionally, some toys could record a child's voice or scan their face. State senator Andrew Gounardes commented that society should not have to live in a Twilight Zone episode turned real, and LaVita Tuff of Mothers Against Media Addiction said parents should be able to feel confident about toy safety, meaning AI-containing toys should only be sold if safe by design. Hochul has emerged as a leading elected campaigner against AI; last month she signed "AI Chatbot Restrictions for Minors" legislation prohibiting companies from offering certain unsafe chatbot features to minors, including those that foster emotional dependency, encourage self-harm, or engage children in sexually explicit talk. The New York measure follows a similar California law placing a four-year moratorium on the sale and manufacture of toys with AI companions. Earlier this week, a consortium of more than 155 child safety advocates and technology experts sent a letter to Amazon CEO Andy Jassy and eBay CEO Jamie Iannone asking them to bar AI toys from their platforms; Rachel Franz, an advocate for limitations on tech for children and leader of a program at the non-profit Fairplay, told NBC News that just as cars are not released without seat belts or rigorous safety testing, toys should be rigorously tested before reaching consumers. An eBay spokesperson said its company continually evaluates policies, engages with regulators, and complies with applicable laws to keep its marketplace safe; an Amazon spokesperson stated it requires third-party sellers to comply with applicable laws and regulations and is committed to the safety of children and families while supporting industry efforts to put guardrails in place as technology develops.
items.title: New York Bans AI-Powered Toys That Talk to Children

items.summary: Following first-ever military attacks on Amazon data centers in the Middle East this year and unprecedented drone strikes between Russia and Ukraine, Ars Technica hosted a live discussion with Tech Reporter Jeremy Hsu and Joseph Jarnecki of the Royal United Services Institute to examine what these attacks mean for cloud services. Jarnecki explained that public and private cloud data centers have increasingly become military targets during the 2026 Iran war and ongoing Russian invasion of Ukraine, because militaries use compute functions within these facilities—such as running battlefield management systems, HR, and resource management—and once a civilian infrastructure is used by an adversary it can become a legitimate target under international law. He also noted that relatively cheap kamikaze drones like the Shahed inflict disproportionate economic costs when striking data centers: he estimated conservatively that the investment in AWS and other companies' Gulf-based installations compared to the cost of Iranian-produced Shahed drones is at least 100X, making it highly lucrative for adversaries. The discussion also covered cloud resilience lessons for governments and hyperscalers including Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and Meta, with Jarnecki highlighting how Ukraine safeguarded its cloud infrastructure when Putin ordered a full-scale invasion in February 2022.
items.title: Ars Live Discussion on Military Attacks on Data Centers

items.summary: EA Sports has created an AI recreation of the late BBC football commentator John 'Motty' Motson, who died in February 2023 after a 50-year career, to provide commentary in its upcoming football simulator game FC27. The broadcaster's family approved the use of the technology, with his son Fred Motson describing it as a touching tribute that preserves his memory and lets new generations experience his legacy; EA Sports is understood to have paid the family for the rights, though the amount was not disclosed. According to the company, the recreation draws on nearly 10 years of recordings from between 1996 and 2006 when Motson commentedated for the game then known as Fifa, combining his original audio with an AI-recreation trained by those recordings. The voice is set to be added via a software update, reportedly featuring commentary about players such as Lamine Yamal and Chloe Kelly. The revival drew criticism from some users on Reddit, who called it disrespectful or gross and likened the broader practice of resurrecting deceased people through AI to 'ghostploitation.' EA Sports noted that this follows similar arrangements involving other figures: in September, Greta Garbo's family licensed her image and voice rights for an AI version appearing in a Swedish industrial company advert, and earlier this year an AI recreation of Val Kilmer was unveiled as the star of As Deep As the Grave, a film he had been cast in but could not complete before his death.
items.title: AI Resurrects John Motson's Voice for EA Sports FC27

items.summary: Kyiv's General Staff said it hit five Russian military aircraft — three MiG-31s and two Su-34s — at the Savasleyka airfield, located 300km (185 miles) east of Moscow in Russia's Nizhny Novgorod region. The extent of the damage was still being assessed as of publication, with no elaboration on the weapons used; Russia had not commented on the strikes.
items.title: Ukraine Claims Airfield Strike Damaged Five Russian Jets

items.summary: A recent study led by Edward Backus and co-authored with Sofía Solórzano found that the resplendent quetzal, an emblematic bird of Mexico and Central America's cloud forests, has lost more than 360,000 hectares of habitat since 1990. Satellite-based modeling revealed a stark contrast between its two subspecies over this period: the northern subspecies (Pharomachrus mocinno mocinno) lost around 51% of its habitat, while the southern subspecies (P. m. costaricensis) lost only 6.6%. The authors estimate that overall species-wide loss totals about 361,000 hectares (roughly 892,000 acres) of potential breeding habitat, a figure they say could warrant uplisting the quetzal from near threatened to vulnerable on the IUCN Red List.
items.title: Study Finds Northern Resplendent Quetzal Losing Half Its Habitat Since 1990

items.summary: Moldova has launched a national emergency preparedness campaign called 'Moldova Ready,' which was introduced in Chisinau amid growing concerns that the war in neighbouring Ukraine is bringing new risks across its border. The campaign features a public display of the remains of a drone that crashed within the country last month, reportedly carrying 52kg of explosives (per q1 [106:110]). FRANCE 24's Daniel Whittington reported on the initiative.
items.title: Moldova launches national preparedness campaign after drone incursions
